  Every sentence on the page is about the reader's notes, the reader's data, the reader's ideas.
- **Who that person is:** *"people who think on paper."* Writers and thinkers working alone.
  There is no collaboration language anywhere on the page — no "share," "invite," "workspace."
  Assume a solo reader until the product says otherwise.

---

## Core traits

### 1. Calm, never urgent

The page has **zero exclamation points and zero questions**. Nothing shouts, nothing sells hard,
nothing counts down. The literal promise words are *calm*, *distraction-free*, *stays out of your
way*, *think clearly*.

> ✅ "A calm, distraction-free editor that stays out of your way so the words can flow."
> ❌ "Supercharge your notes with our blazing-fast editor!"

### 2. Benefit first, mechanism second (or never)

Feature names are written as things **the reader does**, not things the software has:

| On the page | Not |
| --- | --- |
| Write without friction | Minimal editor |
| Find anything instantly | Full-text search engine |
| Stay in control of your data | AES-256 encryption & export API |

"Full-text search" is the only technical term on the entire page, and it is immediately
translated into a human payoff.

### 3. Reassurance is a recurring theme

Three of the page's strongest lines are about *not losing* something — ideas, notes, control:

- "Capture every idea **before it slips away**"
- "so **nothing you wrote is ever truly lost**"
- "Leave whenever you like — **no lock-in**"

Name the reader's quiet anxiety, then close it. This is the brand's emotional engine — don't
drop it when writing new surfaces.

### 4. The assistant is understated

The AI is mentioned exactly once, lowercase, in a subordinate clause: *"let the **assistant**
connect the dots."* It is never "AI," never "AI-powered," never the headline. The reader is the
one thinking; the assistant helps afterward.

> ❌ "AI-powered note-taking, reimagined."
> ✅ "Jot it down, and let the assistant connect the dots."

### 5. Concrete and tactile

Verbs are short and physical: *capture, slips away, jot, flow, connect the dots.* Nouns are
plain: *ideas, thoughts, words, notes, paper.* The register is closer to a good essay than to a
product brochure.

---

## Mechanics

**Capitalization**
- Sentence case everywhere — headings, buttons, nav, feature titles. Only proper nouns are
  capitalized. ("Get started for free", "Stay in control of your data", "Start free".)
- Never Title Case. Never ALL CAPS in authored text. The uppercase eyebrow is a *CSS*
  `text-transform`; the source string is written sentence case ("Notes that think with you").
  Keep authoring it that way.

**Punctuation**
- No terminal period on headings, eyebrows, buttons, or nav. Body sentences take periods.
- **No exclamation points. No question marks.** (0 of each on the page.)
- **No contractions** anywhere in the shipped copy — "nothing you wrote is ever truly lost," not
  "isn't." Treat this as the house style; it's part of why the voice reads settled rather than
  chatty.
- Oxford comma: yes — "connect the dots, suggest the next step, and keep everything searchable."
- **Spaced em dash** for the reassuring turn at the end of a line: "Leave whenever you like — no
  lock-in." Also in the page title: "Lumen Notes — think clearly." Use it sparingly, and use it
  to *relieve* tension, not to add an aside.

**Numbers**
- Spelled out in prose: "the **two**-minute tour," not "2-minute."

**Brand name**
- "**Lumen Notes**" — two words — in all prose and body copy.
- "LumenNotes" set solid is the logo lockup only (with *Notes* in the orange accent). Never use
  the solid form in a sentence.

**Length and rhythm**
- Body sentences run **11–15 words**. Feature descriptions are one sentence; the hero subhead is
  two. If a sentence passes ~20 words, split it.
- Feature headings are 3–6 words.

---

## Two signature sentence patterns

Reuse these; they carry more of the voice than any single word choice.

**1. Mechanism → `so` → human payoff**
> "…stays out of your way **so** the words can flow."
> "Full-text search across every note, **so** nothing you wrote is ever truly lost."

**2. Statement. → em dash → the reassurance**
> "Your notes are encrypted and exportable. Leave whenever you like — no lock-in."

---

## Vocabulary

**Reach for:** capture, jot, flow, clear, calm, quiet, connect, search, find, keep, control,
export, leave, friction, distraction-free, ideas, thoughts, words, paper, instantly, everything,
anything.

**Avoid:** leverage, empower, seamless, robust, revolutionary, game-changing, supercharge,
unlock, 10x, cutting-edge, best-in-class, effortlessly (as filler), "reimagined," "the future
of," AI-powered, "users," "solutions," "harness," urgency framing ("don't miss out," "limited
time"), and any emoji in prose. The page's decorative glyphs (✶ ⚡ ◎) are *visual* elements, not
copy — don't put emoji in sentences.

---

## Calls to action

CTAs on the page: **"Start free"**, **"Get started for free"**, **"Watch the two-minute tour"**.

Rules they encode:
- Sentence case, no period.
- Say "free" plainly when it's free. Twice on this page — no hedging, no asterisk.
- Lower the perceived cost of the click with a **concrete, small number**: "two-minute tour"
  beats "watch demo" because it tells you exactly what you're agreeing to.
- Start with a verb the reader performs: *start, get, watch*.

---

## Extending to surfaces the page doesn't cover

*Extrapolated from the traits above — treat as a starting point, not as observed evidence.*

- **Empty states:** invite, don't nag. "Nothing here yet. Jot down the first thing on your mind."
- **Errors:** state what happened, then what is safe. Lead with reassurance, since that is the
  brand's core move. "That note did not save. Your text is still here — try again in a moment."
  Never blame the reader, never use "invalid" or "failed" at them.
- **Confirmations:** short and undramatic. "Saved." Not "Success! Your note has been saved!"
- **Destructive actions:** be plain about consequences and honor the no-lock-in promise —
  "Deleting removes this note from every device. You can export first."
- **Email/onboarding:** same third-person product voice, same no-urgency rule. No "⏰ Last chance."

---

## What the landing page does not tell us

Flagging these so nobody invents an answer and calls it the voice:

- **Collaboration and team language** — entirely absent. If a team feature ships, the "you"
  address and solo-thinker framing will need a deliberate decision.
- **Pricing tone** — there's a Pricing nav item but no pricing copy. "Free" is stated warmly;
  how the paid tier is framed is undecided.
- **Long-form voice** — there's a Blog nav item but no long-form sample. All evidence here is
  short-form. Assume the same register, but the sentence-length rules above are calibrated to
  marketing copy, not essays.
- **Humor** — the page is warm but never jokes. The closest thing to personality is the footer,
  *"Made for people who think on paper."* That's the ceiling: affectionate, dry, one line.
- **The no-contractions rule** rests on a small sample (roughly 90 words of prose). It's
  consistent across all of it, so it's stated as a rule — but it's the single item here most
  worth confirming against any other copy you have.

---

## Quick check before shipping copy

1. Any exclamation points, questions, or contractions? Remove them.
2. Is it Title Case? Make it sentence case.
3. Does it name a feature, or name what the reader gets? Prefer the second.
4. Does it say "AI"? Say "the assistant," or say nothing.
5. Over ~20 words? Split it.
6. Read it aloud — does it sound calm, or does it sound like it's selling? Calm wins.
7. Would "people who think on paper" recognize themselves in it?

#!/bin/bash
# Merge the vendor's returned French XLIFF back into report.docx.
#
#   ./merge-back.sh <returned-report.docx.xlf> [output-dir]
#
# Runs pre-merge QA on the XLIFF, merges with Okapi Tikal using the original
# report.docx, restores the fr-FR proofing language, then verifies the result.

set -euo pipefail

XLF="${1:?usage: ./merge-back.sh <returned.xlf> [output-dir]}"
OUTDIR="${2:-fr-FR}"
HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
TIKAL="${TIKAL:-$HOME/src/neokapi/neokapi/.parity/tikal/tikal.sh}"

[ -f "$HERE/report.docx" ] || { echo "report.docx not found next to this script"; exit 1; }
[ -x "$TIKAL" ] || { echo "tikal not found at $TIKAL — set TIKAL=/path/to/tikal.sh"; exit 1; }

mkdir -p "$OUTDIR" "$HERE/.tmp"
# Okapi's OpenXML writer needs a writable temp dir; keep it local and predictable.
export _JAVA_OPTIONS="-Djava.io.tmpdir=$HERE/.tmp"

echo "==> Pre-merge QA on $XLF"
python3 - "$XLF" <<'PY'
import sys
from lxml import etree
X = "urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:document:1.2"
t = etree.parse(sys.argv[1])
empty, mismatch, total = [], [], 0
for tu in t.iter(f"{{{X}}}trans-unit"):
    total += 1
    tid = tu.get("id")
    src, tgt = tu.find(f"{{{X}}}source"), tu.find(f"{{{X}}}target")
    if tgt is None or not "".join(tgt.itertext()).strip():
        empty.append(tid); continue
    codes = lambda e: sorted(c.tag.split('}')[1] + (c.get("id") or "")
                             for c in e.iter() if c is not e)
    if codes(src) != codes(tgt):
        mismatch.append(f"{tid}: source {codes(src)} vs target {codes(tgt)}")
print(f"    {total} trans-units, {total - len(empty)} translated")
for tid in empty:    print(f"    UNTRANSLATED: {tid}")
for m in mismatch:   print(f"    INLINE-CODE MISMATCH: {m}")
sys.exit(1 if (empty or mismatch) else 0)
PY

echo "==> Merging into DOCX"
"$TIKAL" -m "$XLF" -sd "$HERE" -od "$OUTDIR" -sl en-US -tl fr-FR 2>&1 \
  | sed 's/\x1b\[[0-9;]*m//g' | grep -iE "Output:|Error|Done in" || true

MERGED="$OUTDIR/$(basename "${XLF%.xlf}")"
[ -f "$MERGED" ] || { echo "merge produced no file"; exit 1; }

echo "==> Restoring fr-FR proofing language"
# Okapi sets themeFontLang to fr-FR but drops <w:lang> from docDefaults; without it
# Word spell-checks the French text against whatever the reader's default language is.
python3 - "$MERGED" <<'PY'
import shutil, sys, zipfile
path = sys.argv[1]
LANG = b'<w:lang w:val="fr-FR" w:eastAsia="zh-CN" w:bidi="ar-SA"/>'
src = zipfile.ZipFile(path)
items = [(i, src.read(i.filename)) for i in src.infolist()]
src.close()
patched = False
for idx, (info, data) in enumerate(items):
    if info.filename == "word/styles.xml" and b"<w:lang" not in data:
        data = data.replace(b"</w:rPr></w:rPrDefault>", LANG + b"</w:rPr></w:rPrDefault>", 1)
        items[idx] = (info, data); patched = data.count(LANG) == 1
with zipfile.ZipFile(path + ".new", "w", zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as out:
    for info, data in items:
        out.writestr(info, data)
shutil.move(path + ".new", path)
print("    docDefaults w:lang -> fr-FR" if patched else "    w:lang already present, left as-is")
PY

echo "==> Verifying $MERGED"
python3 - "$MERGED" <<'PY'
import sys, zipfile
from lxml import etree
z = zipfile.ZipFile(sys.argv[1])
assert z.testzip() is None, "corrupt zip"
parts = [n for n in z.namelist() if n.endswith((".xml", ".rels"))]

    etree.fromstring(z.read(n))
lang = b'w:val="fr-FR"' in z.read("word/settings.xml")
print(f"    OK — {len(z.namelist())} parts, {len(parts)} XML parts well-formed, themeFontLang fr-FR: {lang}")
PY
echo "==> Done: $MERGED"

# i18n

A small, dependency-free translation layer (no network access to install
`react-i18next` in this environment). The public API deliberately mirrors
i18next's, so swapping the implementation later is mostly a matter of deleting
`translate.js` / `I18nProvider.jsx` and re-pointing `index.js`.

## Usage

```jsx
const { t, locale, setLocale, dir } = useTranslation();

t("nav.tasks");                        // plain lookup
t("home.greeting", { name: "Alex" });  // {{name}} interpolation
t("home.tasksDue", { count });         // plural selection
```

`<I18nProvider>` wraps the app in `App.jsx`. It detects the locale from
`localStorage` → `navigator.languages` → `en`, persists the user's choice, and
keeps `<html lang>` / `<html dir>` in sync.

## Adding a key

Add it to every catalog in `locales/`. Keys are flat, dot-namespaced strings.

For countable messages, add one entry per [CLDR plural category] the language
uses (`_one`, `_other`, plus `_few` / `_many` etc. where relevant) — the
category is picked by `Intl.PluralRules`. An optional `_zero` entry is used at
`count === 0` even in languages whose CLDR rules have no `zero` category, which
is how English gets "You have no tasks due today."

Numbers passed as interpolation values are formatted with `Intl.NumberFormat`
for the active locale.

## Adding a locale

1. Copy `locales/en.js` to `locales/<code>.js` and translate the values.
2. Register it in `LOCALES` in `config.js` with a native-language `label` and
   its writing `dir` (`"rtl"` is honoured throughout).

Missing translations fall back to English, then to the key itself, with a
console warning outside production.

[CLDR plural category]: https://cldr.unicode.org/index/cldr-spec/plural-rules

# i18n Zero-dependency translation layer built on the platform `Intl` APIs. ## Using a string in a component ```jsx import { useTranslation } from './i18n/index.jsx'; function Greeting({ user, count }) { const { t } = useTranslation(); return ( <>

{t('dashboard.greeting', { name: user.name })}

{t('dashboard.tasksDueToday', { count })}

); } ``` `useTranslation()` also returns `locale` and `dir`, and must be called inside ``. The provider picks the locale from the browser unless you pass one: ``. ## Writing messages Messages live in `messages/.js`, keyed by `feature.name`. ```js 'tasks.add': 'Add a task', // plain 'dashboard.greeting': 'Welcome back, {name}', // {placeholder} 'dashboard.tasksDueToday': { // plural, selected by `count` one: 'You have {count} task due today.', other: 'You have {count} tasks due today.', }, ``` Numbers passed as values are formatted for the active locale (`12345` renders as `12,345` in `en`, `12.345` in `es`). Rules that keep strings translatable: - **Never concatenate.** `t('greeting') + name` breaks any language where word order differs. Use a placeholder instead. - **Never branch on count in JSX.** `count === 1 ? … : …` assumes English plural rules; Arabic has six categories, Japanese has one. Use a plural message — `Intl.PluralRules` picks the right form per locale. - **Keep data out of the catalog.** Names, titles, and other user content are values, not copy. - **One key per concept, not per screen.** Reuse `tasks.add` everywhere the action appears, but don't reuse a key just because two strings happen to match in English — they may diverge elsewhere. ## Adding a locale 1. Copy `messages/en.js` to `messages/.js` and translate the values, leaving the keys untouched. 2. Register it in `index.jsx`: ```js import fr from './messages/fr.js'; export const catalogs = { en, es, fr }; ``` Adjust plural forms to that language's CLDR categories (`zero`, `one`, `two`, `few`, `many`, `other`) — see the [CLDR plural rules chart](https://www.unicode.org/cldr/charts/47/supplemental/language_plural_rules.html). A locale only needs the categories its language actually uses; missing keys fall back to English and log a warning in development. RTL languages set `` automatically — use CSS logical properties (`margin-inline-start`, not `margin-left`) so layouts mirror correctly.
